t: The twenty-two boxes
sub: Marie Curie's desk on the fourth floor at five to eight: one disbursement instruction on the old LOS green screen, and the printout of it she keeps face up beside the keyboard.
head: LOS · DISBURSEMENT INSTRUCTION · third tranche · EUR 250,000,000 · value date Monday
sheet: Green characters on black, one screen of twenty-two boxes — and a paper copy, because the screen cannot be carried to a meeting

items.d: Which loan agreement this payment belongs to. Everything else hangs off it.
The euro area member state receiving the money.
Which of the ESM's lending products this is — a programme loan, a credit line, a bank recapitalisation.
Loans are paid out in parts. This is the third part.
Two hundred and fifty million. One mistyped digit here is the reason a second officer reads all three screens.
Always EUR, and typed three times anyway.
The day the money must actually sit in the receiving account. Monday. It is the only date anybody outside this floor cares about.
When the member state formally asked.
Twenty-seven characters, re-keyed into two other systems by hand. This is the field everybody is frightened of.
The receiving bank's code.
The ESM's own account at another bank, out of which the money leaves. Step 31 of the process map is a telephone call to check it is funded.
How interest is calculated — day count, floating or fixed.
The ESM's charge on top of its own cost of funding. A basis point is one hundredth of one per cent.
Derived from the value date. If the value date moves, this moves, and so does the whole repayment schedule.
Points at the table of dates on which the country pays back.
Which pool of issued bonds funded this tranche. It decides what the loan costs.
How the cost of the bonds is shared out over the loans. The two loans that fail to reconcile in April 2028 fail on exactly this.
The lawyers' confirmation that the drawdown is validly requested.
Money arrives only when the agreed reforms have been reviewed. This box says which review.
Who released it. One of the two audit findings is about this box and the next one.
A different person reads all three systems against each other and signs. In 2028 the platform refuses instead of a person reading.
The daily cut-off. An instruction that arrives after four o'clock loses its value date, and nobody in the building has ever written down why.

notes: What you are looking at

A disbursement instruction is the order that moves money out of the ESM to a member state. In January 2026 it exists three times: once in LOS, once in the treasury system, once in the payment gateway. Marie Curie types the same twenty-two boxes into all three.
Where the numbers in the story come from

Twenty-two fields, re-keyed twice, is about 1,400 fields a quarter. That is success criterion SC4, and its target is zero. On 18 January 2029 she types the boxes once and is finished in forty seconds.
Why anyone cares

Five working days from instruction to value date, three more to reconcile afterwards, and two open internal-audit findings — segregation of duties, and the completeness of the audit trail — all live on this one screen.

t: The five numbers, on one card
sub: Printed off the Business Case and taped inside the front cover of the Project Charter; Florence Nightingale keeps a copy in the folder she carries to every meeting.
head: Measurable success criteria · Business Case §3 · carried word for word into Project Charter §3.2
sheet: One card, A5, printed. The only page of this project that everybody can quote from memory

items.t: Disbursement cycle time, instruction to value date — five working days down to one
items.d: How long it takes from the moment an instruction is complete to the moment the money must be in the account. Marie Curie's objection is that the five days are not idle: somebody checks, somebody else releases, and they are never the same person.

items.t: Post-disbursement reconciliation — three working days down to same day
items.d: Reconciliation means proving that what the ESM thinks it paid and what the banks say it paid are the same. On 11 April 2027 it takes two days and Grace Hopper says out loud that she owns that sentence.

items.t: New instrument onboarding — nine months down to six weeks
items.d: How long it takes to make a brand-new kind of loan possible in the system. Today it means writing code. The point of the whole project is that it should mean filling in a form. It is the one criterion nobody can prove by July 2028, because no new instrument arrives.

items.t: Manual re-keying of payment instructions — about 1,400 fields a quarter down to zero
items.d: The twenty-two boxes, typed twice more, counted over three months. Two people counted them in December 2025 and it took a morning. The same two people count them again in 2028.

items.t: Open internal-audit findings on LOS — two down to zero
items.d: Internal Audit raised two findings: segregation of duties, and the completeness of the audit trail. Florence Nightingale signs the response to both every year. The closure letter arrives on 4 July 2028.

notes: Why five numbers and not a paragraph

A success criterion has to be measurable by somebody who was not in the room. Each of these has a baseline you can check and a target you can miss. Everything else in the project — the tender, the acceptance criteria, the final report — is traced back to one of these five lines.
Baseline and target
The left-hand number is what is true today, the right-hand number is what has to be true afterwards. Without the left-hand number nobody can prove afterwards that anything changed.
The trap at the end

Four of the five are demonstrated by July 2028. None of the five is signed off, because signing them off takes a year of ordinary operating. That is normal, and it is the hardest sentence in the Project-End Report.

t: The one page
sub: Grace Hopper's screen on the Monday morning of 12 January 2026, and the same page printed and lying in front of Lorenzo de' Medici ten days later.
head: Project Initiation Request · CASTOR · v1.0 · 12 Jan 2026
stamp: APPROVED — Corporate Investment Board, item 7, 22 Jan 2026 at 11:14
fields: F. Nightingale, Head of Lending Operations Division
L. da Vinci, Head of IT and Digital Division
Corporate Investment Board, chaired by L. de' Medici
Project folder · 01 Initiating · v1.0 · one place, one version

body.t: CASTOR — Renewal of the Lending Operations System. A castor is a beaver: it builds things and it works at night. The name is provisional, and everything provisional survives forever.
LOS is fourteen years old. Disbursement instructions are re-keyed by hand between three systems. Every new instrument needs bespoke code. Two internal-audit findings are open against it.
About EUR 8.4 million all in. Three thousand one hundred person-days. Twenty-six months. Leonardo da Vinci's estimate, sent at 09:12, with the word indicative in it twice.
Mix. An in-house core team, with the platform implementation bought outside. The four choices on the form are in-house, outsourced, mix, or not known — and not known is a real answer at this stage.
15 May 2028. Florence Nightingale put her head round the door and said write it down. It goes in as a target, not a promise. The day it becomes a promise there is a Charter under it.

Five working days to one. Three days to same day. Nine months to six weeks. Two open audit findings to zero. The 1,400 re-keyed fields are deliberately left for the Business Case, so this stays one page.

Ratification of the Treaty reform is not complete, so the common backstop is a planned capability rather than a live one and the scope can move underneath the project. It is in the public ratification table either way.
Not the money. Not a platform, not a supplier. Authority to spend six weeks finding out whether EUR 8.4 million is the right number — which is a Business Case.
At this amount, the Corporate Investment Board. A smaller request could be accepted by the Project Owner herself and finished by lunch.
Filled in before anybody signs anything. Version 1.0, in the project folder — not an attachment in three mailboxes with three different dates on it.

notes: What a Project Initiation Request is

The first artefact of a project, and usually the shortest. It captures a request while it is still an idea: who wants it, roughly what it costs, roughly how long, and what the requestor thinks success would look like. It does not commit the money.
Why one page matters
It is read by people who see forty of these a year. At eight and a half pages nobody reaches the ask. Lorenzo de' Medici's first sentence in the room is thank you for the one page.
What approving it actually released
Six weeks of a small team's time to write a Business Case — no more. The project still does not exist when everybody leaves the room.

t: Item seven, eleven minutes
sub: The printed agenda at each of twenty-two places in room A1-02, the good room with the working microphones, on the morning of 22 January 2026.
head: Corporate Investment Board · 22 Jan 2026, 11:00 · room A1-02 · nine items · chair: L. de' Medici
sheet: One sheet of A4 per place, plus a decision column the chair fills in himself

items.t: Minutes of the meeting of 11 December 2025
items.d: Two minutes. Nobody objects to minutes.
Twelve projects, one page each. This is the portfolio that CASTOR wants to join.
The project that will be slipped by twelve months in March to make room for CASTOR. Nobody in the room knows that yet, including Leonardo da Vinci, who will suggest it.
Somebody else's project asking for more money, which is what most of these items are.
Administrative budget, like everything on this agenda.
Information only. No decision.
Eleven minutes. The request is not for EUR 8.4 million; it is for authority to write a Business Case. It carries at 11:14.
The item the Board moves to at 11:14, which is the most useful thing anybody could say about how large a project feels to the people funding it.
Where the question nobody prepared for gets asked.

notes: What this board is

The Corporate Investment Board decides which internal projects get money out of the ESM's administrative budget. In PM2 terms it is the Appropriate Governance Body: the layer above the project that owns the portfolio, not the project.
Why the item number matters

A bare item seven is what people quote in corridors afterwards. It means: seventh of nine, eleven minutes, between a cyber update and bicycle parking. That is the real weight of the decision in the life of the person taking it.
The question that comes back

Lorenzo de' Medici asks what leaves the portfolio to make room. Nothing on this agenda is free, and the envelope was allocated in October. In March the answer is item three, costed, with the consequence written next to it.

t: Three ways to spend eight point four million
sub: The file room on the fourth floor, no window and the best whiteboard on the floor: three alternatives in three columns, with Ada Lovelace's process maps taped to the cabinet beside them.
head: Business Case · CASTOR · alternatives, and the two sections that decide it

cards.t: Keep LOS. Spend nothing.
cards.d: Every business case has a do-nothing option. It is not a joke option: it is the baseline everything else is measured against.

cards.t: EUR 0 of project money
cards.d: And the cost that is not project money: both audit findings stay open, onboarding stays at nine months, re-keying stays at about 1,400 fields a quarter, and LOS gets a year older.

cards.t: Written out honestly, it argues against itself
cards.d: Which is exactly why it stays in the document. An option removed before it is written down is an option somebody will propose again in November.

cards.t: Rebuild LOS on modern technology and keep extending it
cards.d: The knowledge stays inside the building. Nikola Tesla's option, and he asks to defend it before it is buried.

cards.t: Cheaper than C, and slower to matter
cards.d: Lower cash cost, longer to first benefit, and the three people who can read the parts of LOS that matter are still three people, two of whom are contractors.

cards.t: Tesla: nothing you buy will do our value-date logic
cards.d: A real argument, made by the person who knows the system best. Albert Einstein asks which problem it solves. The answer — continuity — is not the problem on the wall.

cards.t: Weakness: it keeps bespoke code for every instrument
cards.d: The SWOT is where an option's own weakness is written by its own advocates. B keeps the thing the project exists to remove. It stays in the document as a real option that is simply not the recommendation.

cols.t: C · Configure a market platform — recommended

cards.t: Buy a configurable lending platform and configure it. Delivery: mix.
cards.d: An in-house core team keeps requirements, testing, the two interfaces and anything touching the audit trail. The licence, the implementation and fourteen years of data migration are bought outside.

cards.t: EUR 8.4 m · 3,100 person-days · 26 months
cards.d: The project cost. This is the number that goes into the Charter in March and gets proved line by line in the Work Plan in June.

cards.t: Five-year total cost of ownership
cards.d: Project cost plus licence, maintenance, support and training over five years. It is a bigger number than EUR 8.4 m, and it is the one Lorenzo de' Medici will actually read, because he pays for the years after the project as well.

cards.t: Benefits from 2029, not from go-live
cards.d: Straight-through processing starts on 15 May 2028. The measured benefit is a number Grace Hopper reads out of ordinary operational reporting in 2030.

cols.t: The evidence, and the two sections that decide it

cards.t: 2.2 Current situation impact — forty-one steps
cards.d: Ada Lovelace's six process maps, taped to the cabinet and numbered in the corner: forty-one steps from a signed loan agreement to a value date. Nine of them exist only because two systems cannot speak to each other.

cards.t: Step thirty-one: the back office telephones treasury
cards.d: To confirm that the nostro account — the ESM's own account at another bank — has the money in it. Telephones. In 2026. It is the single line that makes the case without an adjective.

cards.t: 5.12 Synergies and interdependencies — empty until March
cards.d: The section for what this project does to the other projects. Left empty, Lorenzo de' Medici fills it in out loud in the meeting. Filled in, it says: the reporting warehouse refresh slips from 2026 into 2027, at a cost of two quarters of manual regulatory extracts, about ninety person-days of Finance and Control time.

cards.t: The recommendation: C, with the price of the trade-off beside it
cards.d: Approved by the Corporate Investment Board on 24 March 2026 in nineteen minutes, most of which were about the reporting warehouse. After that, the question of whether to build is closed — although it takes four more drafts of the Outsourcing Plan for everybody to believe it.

notes: What a Business Case is for

Not to argue for the thing somebody already wants. It sets out the problem, then several ways of solving it, each costed and each with its own strengths and weaknesses, and then recommends one of them with reasons a stranger can check.
Why do-nothing and the losing options stay in

Because the decision is only as good as the alternatives it beat. In September 2026 a bidder will read the tender file; in 2028 an auditor will read the Business Case. Both need to see what was not chosen, and why.
Three, not four

The gate checklist asks whether at least four alternatives were analysed. CASTOR analysed three, and Grace Hopper refuses to invent a fourth. That single unticked box is the whole argument about whether a checklist is a treaty or a tool.

t: The Charter, open at the last page
sub: Twenty-odd printed pages in B4-12 on the morning of 24 March 2026, turned over to the signature block, with Florence Nightingale's pen already out.
head: Project Charter · CASTOR · v1.0 · 24 Mar 2026
stamp: Accepted by the Project Steering Committee 24 Mar 2026 · corporate approval by the Corporate Investment Board the same afternoon, in nineteen minutes
fields: CASTOR — Renewal of the Lending Operations System
F. Nightingale, Head of Lending Operations
L. da Vinci, Head of IT and Digital
G. Hopper, Senior Loan Operations Officer
EUR 8.4 m · 3,100 person-days · 26 months · delivery: mix

body.t: Replace LOS with a configurable lending operations platform delivering straight-through processing from loan agreement to disbursement to repayment schedule, with instrument-agnostic product configuration, same-day automated reconciliation and a complete audit trail.

SC1 to SC5, quoted from the Business Case rather than paraphrased. The reconciliation target had drifted to next day in an early draft, because somebody copied an old table. Deming caught it. It reads same day. Two documents, one baseline.

The treasury system. The payment messaging gateway. Bespoke screens for the common backstop to the Single Resolution Fund. Said loudly, because people hear new system and assume their own thing goes with it. The backstop arrives as configuration if it arrives at all, which is how the project stops being hostage to a ratification nobody in this building controls.

D-01 configuration engine. D-02 straight-through disbursement. D-03 a parallel run that proves both. D-04 forty loan administrators trained. D-05 a decommissioned LOS. D-04 is the first time in fourteen years that training people has been on the same list as software.

Four eyes has to survive the automation: if straight-through means one officer can originate and release the same disbursement, one audit finding closes and a worse one opens. It is a feature traced to a deliverable, not a footnote. And the audit trail holds staff identifiers and counterparty contact details, so it is also a processing operation under data protection — written down in March, not discovered in June.

EUR 8.4 million across 2026 to 2028. Three thousand one hundred person-days internal. Type of delivery: mix. Administrative budget — it does not touch the ESM's lending capacity or its paid-in capital.
Ready for Executing 3 Jul 2026. Contract award 18 Sep 2026. Release 1 26 Mar 2027. Release 2 17 Dec 2027. Parallel run 8 Jan to 30 Apr 2028. Go-live 15 May 2028.

R-07, loss of the contractor's key architect: high likelihood, high impact, named in March so that procurement can price a key-person clause in September. Ratification of the Treaty reform. Lending Operations releasing its people for two years.
PM2, no deviations. The shortest paragraph in the document and the one people argue about longest.

Who does what, by name. Marie Curie, User Representative, reviews and signs off the requirements — written here with her name against it, so that pointing at a document is not a polite way of forgetting it.

Two hundred and twelve requirements do not go in a document meant to be read in twenty minutes. The Charter carries high-level needs and features and points at the Requirements Document, by reference, with a document location. If it lives on the analyst's own drive it does not exist.

notes: What a Project Charter is

The document that turns an approved idea into a project. It fixes the scope, the success criteria, the money, the dates, the risks and the people, and it is the thing every later argument is measured against. The Business Case says why; the Charter says what.
The trap in the signature block

Florence Nightingale is the Project Owner, she is paying for it and she has read it twice — and it is still not hers alone to sign. The Charter is accountable to the Project Steering Committee, which she chairs but is not. A chair signing on behalf of a committee that has not been asked is the same signature with none of the protection.
Why quoting beats paraphrasing

Section 3.2 repeats the Business Case's criteria word for word. The one time somebody paraphrased — same day became next day — it survived two drafts and was caught by an independent reviewer four days before signature.

extra: Two hundred and twelve, then two hundred and fourteen

Two hundred and twelve on 17 March 2026, after six workshops that Marie Curie's people signed every sheet of. Two hundred and fourteen by 21 May, because requirements keep arriving. The number in the Charter is the number on the day the Charter was written, and that is fine as long as the document it points at carries the current one.
Requirement 104, in Marie Curie's words

The instrument list shows the six instruments in this order, PCCL above ECCL, and the field is eleven characters wide. That is a screen. It is what they asked for and it is what they drew — and if it is written down as the requirement, then in 2029 a seventh instrument means bespoke code again.
Requirement 104, priced
Nine person-days if the presentation order is configurable. Two person-days if the list is fixed. Nikola Tesla would take the nine.
MoSCoW

Must, Should, Could, Won't. A Must is a requirement without which the project does not go live on 15 May 2028. Say that sentence over all ninety-six and about twenty move on their own. Won't is a decision, not a refusal: it means not this time, and it is written down so nobody re-argues it in 2027.
The six states

Specified, Proposed, Approved, Incorporated, Implemented, Validated. Approved is the line that changes everything, because after it those requirements are the scope, and anything new is a change with a form and a number.
notes: What a Requirements Document is

The list of what the thing has to do, written so that it can be built, tested and argued about one line at a time. It is not the Charter: the Charter carries high-level needs and points here, because two hundred and twelve numbered lines cannot be read in twenty minutes by people who do not work on this floor.
Need, not button

A Refresh button at the top right is a solution shaped like a button. The need underneath it — I have to know the queue in front of me is the queue that exists — can be satisfied three ways, and one of them costs nothing because it is already in the product. The button goes in the notes as the thing that prompted the requirement.
Why the priorities are fought over
Ninety-six Musts is not a prioritisation, it is a wish list with a ribbon on it. Priorities are what turns a list into a plan when the money and the dates stop stretching.

extra: Initiating sheet, 27 Mar 2026
Twenty-eight questions, one unticked. Ninety-six per cent.
Planning sheet, 3 Jul 2026
Forty-three checks. Compliance ninety-eight per cent, status 0.9. Two answers are not Yes. Above eighty per cent on the template's own scale — and it does not mean anything else.
Executing sheet, 22 Jun 2028
Ninety-seven per cent, status 0.9. Answered by the Project Manager, assured by Quality Assurance, and it approves nothing by itself.
Stakeholders sheet, planning phase
Ninety per cent, signed at the gate on 3 Jul 2026. Ninety is the part everybody already knows. The ten is the meeting.
Who owns a checklist
The Deliverables Acceptance Checklist has no responsibility row anywhere in the guide. Nobody approves it. It is the Project Manager's control tool and it lives with him.
notes: What a phase gate actually asks

Not whether the documents are approved — that was Tuesday. It asks whether the project is in a fit state to start the next phase. On 24 March the Corporate Investment Board approved everything; three days later the same people sat down and asked a different question.
Yes, partially, no
A checklist row is not a school report. Partially is the honest answer to most real questions, and the useful part is the comment: who, by when. Rows that say no take a date, not a verdict.
The percentage at the bottom

Ninety-eight per cent and status 0.9 mean the sheet is above the template's own eighty per cent threshold. They do not mean the thing will work. Nothing in forty-three checks asks whether the platform will work — that is what the next two years are for.

cards.t: R-07 · Loss of the contractor's key architect
cards.d: Opened in the Charter in March 2026, before there was a contract or an architect to lose — which is precisely when it is cheap. External. Owner Leonardo da Vinci. The parallel run is January to April 2028 and there is an EFSF bond rollover inside that window; her people cannot do both, and she has already been told which one comes second. notes: Four registers, one distinction

A risk might happen; an issue has happened and needs a management action. A decision records what was settled, by whom, and from when. A change is anything that moves the baselined scope, schedule, cost or quality. The moment a risk materialises it leaves one log and opens in another, and the old entry closes with the reason written into it.
Why not the minutes

Minutes are the record of a meeting. A log is the record of the thing. Only one of them is read by somebody who was not there — which is how a Committee decision on R-07 in October 2026 was still missing from the Risk Log six months later.
What gets logged

Not everything that goes wrong. Only what cannot be sorted out easily and needs a management action. Small ones close with the Business Manager; medium and above go to the Steering Committee, and the decision lands in the Decision Log with a name against it.

Six management plans, four separate documents. Requirements, issue, quality and communications each get their own document. Risk and change stay as sections 4.1 and 4.4 of this book, because a section is enough for them here and a separate plan would only ever be read by the Project Manager. It is a decision, written where somebody can argue with it.

Very low and low, the Core Team decides. Medium, the Business Manager and the Project Manager decide at the status meeting. High and very high go to the Steering Committee. It lives here once, and every other plan points at it instead of copying it. A disagreement is worked where it arises, in writing, for five working days, with both managers copied. On the sixth day it goes up.

Scoring, appetite, categories and the escalation bands. Likelihood times impact, each one to five. Risk level six or below is inside the appetite. Nothing above one chance in four. Nothing where the loss could run past two per cent of the budget — EUR 168,000.

How far a number may move before somebody else has to hear about it. Anything over ten working days of forecast slip goes to the Steering Committee. On 31 March 2027 the go-live forecast moves by a month, and that is what puts the recovery plan on the agenda of the twenty-third whether or not anybody likes its shape by then.

Any deviation from the scope, schedule, cost or quality baselined in June. Size and priority both scored one to five. Very low and low, the Business Manager and Project Manager decide; medium and above, the Steering Committee sits as the change control board. Four outcomes, not two: approve, reject, postpone, merge. Postponed is an honest answer, which is why nothing has to be smuggled in — and why a request made in a lift can be answered by a form with a number on it.
How people leave. Contractor staff are released when the parallel run ends on 30 April 2028. Written in 2026 so that in 2028 it is a plan and not a negotiation.

What gets counted, in the same shape every time: critical path tasks and the ones about to become critical; deliverables finished and verified; days burned against days planned; and the four logs. A task is at zero or at a hundred, and it reaches a hundred when somebody who did not build it says so. Nobody on CASTOR types the same number into two systems: the contractor's sprint data is reshaped by the Project Support Office.

notes: What a Project Handbook is

The rulebook for one project: the approach, the controlling processes, the escalation route, the tailoring of the method, and who holds which role. It is written once, in Planning, and then everybody argues with it instead of with each other.
Why it is the book everybody ignores, correctly

Nobody reads forty-one pages twice. The value is that when a disagreement happens in month nineteen, the answer already exists in a document that was approved before anybody knew who would be on which side of it.
Tailoring is a decision, not a shortcut

Deciding that risk and change live as sections rather than as separate plans is allowed — as long as it is written where somebody can object. A shortcut nobody can see is the thing an auditor finds in 2028.

notes: What RASCI is for

A table with one row per document or activity and one column per role. It exists to settle, in advance and in public, the two questions that otherwise get settled by seniority in the room: who does this, and whose name is on it if it goes wrong.
The four plans everyone forgets

The Outsourcing Plan, the Deliverables Acceptance Plan, the Transition Plan and the Business Implementation Plan are approved by four different people — the governance body, the committee, the committee again, and the Project Owner on her own. The Project Manager approves none of them. He writes three and supports the fourth.
Why it keeps surprising people
Because accountability follows the consequence, not the effort. The person who spent three weeks writing a plan is usually R. The person who will be sitting opposite the auditors is A.

Two scales on one grid

notes: Why a naming convention is a control and not tidiness
A file name is the only thing that survives the person who wrote the file. Version, date and project in the name mean that a document found in 2031 can be placed without asking anybody who was there.
The question it answers

Which document does the rule live in?

notes: What a Work Plan is

The breakdown of the work, with an estimate, a resource and a date against every piece of it, added up. It is the first document in the project that can be wrong in a way that costs money, and the first one that can prove the Charter's figure rather than repeat it.

The platform licence. The implementation. Migration of fourteen years of LOS data. Two releases.
Requirements. Testing. The two interfaces. And anything that touches the audit trail — which is the sentence the Solution Provider came for.

body.t: EUR 8.4 million, all in. If the tender comes back at nine, it goes back to the Corporate Investment Board, because that is the body whose money it is.

The existing framework contract covers staff augmentation and infrastructure — it is how the contractor's own architect is already paid. It does not cover a licensed lending platform with implementation and fourteen years of migration, so there is no mini-competition to run. Open tender under the procurement code, section 3.1, two paragraphs. Four months, and those four months are already in the schedule.

Taken from the Charter, not from a vendor demonstration in Amsterdam. Onboard a new instrument in six weeks — SC3, down from nine months. Zero manual re-keying — SC4, down from about 1,400 fields a quarter. Neither sentence names anybody. Six weeks reads generously beside the forty minutes one sales engineer took on a stage, and a target does not move because somebody was quick. The headings are weighted before an envelope is opened, not after.

The contractor's own architect is not on it. Written into the plan in May 2026, while it is still nothing, rather than in September when it would be a favour. His architecture note stays in the file, and goes to every bidder on the same morning with everything else he has seen since January.

The Project Manager is the sole interface. The contractor's Project Manager reports to him, and escalates to the Steering Committee if he has to. The Project Manager approves timesheets and purchase orders. The Project Owner accepts deliverables. The governance body authorises the award. Nobody talks to the contractor's engineers except through their own project manager.

The contractor's status report reaches the Project Manager by the fifth of each month. When it is late it is late because the contractor is late. It does not go to the Steering Committee; it goes into the one-page Status Report as four lines, under the Project Manager's name. Squeezing a supplier on paper, dated, against the working methods written here, is what the plan is for — and it is what a supplier's own project manager would rather have than a reorganisation by his account director.

Configuration manuals. An operations runbook. The migration mapping. The interface specifications. Named as deliverables, so that in 2028 they are an obligation and not a favour. The manuals go to the forty administrators, to the support team and to the bidders with the tender, so that nobody meets them for the first time on the day they are asked to sign.

Step seven of the acceptance process: what the contract says about acceptance is what acceptance is. The tender file closes in July and the contract is signed on 18 September — so an acceptance plan approved after that describes a process the contractor never agreed to. Approved 26 June, in the tender file in July.

Ten per cent held back until final acceptance. Held against a reconciliation number that partly depends on the quality of the ESM's own data — which no serious bidder prices without a caveat, and the caveat may cost more than the retention is worth. Whatever is decided, what is owed to the supplier is written down: a retention against a number you only half control is a dispute with a date on it.

notes: What an Outsourcing Plan is

The document that decides what is bought rather than built, how a supplier is chosen, who may talk to them, what they must hand over, and how they are paid. It is written before the tender, because everything in it has to be true in the contract.
Why the governance body is accountable

When an award goes wrong nobody asks the project. They ask the floor that authorised it, in a room with the auditors, how a contractor was chosen. The Project Owner approves the Business Case, the Charter, the Handbook, the acceptance plan, the transition plan and the business implementation plan — and not this one.
Reviewing is not being accountable

The Solution Provider is Supporting on the one plan that decides who builds his platform, and accountable afterwards for what that contractor produces. Those are two different sentences, and everybody has to hear both of them said out loud once.

notes: What a Deliverables Acceptance Plan is

The agreement, written before anything exists, about what good will look like and who gets to say so. Metric, tolerance, approver — three things per criterion. Without them, acceptance is a conversation between tired people on a Friday afternoon.
Why it is written two years early

Because criteria written in 2027, when there is something in front of you, get written to fit whatever arrived. The objection is fair — you are agreeing what good looks like before you have seen anything at all — and the answer is that this is the only moment when nobody has anything to defend.
Explained is not resolved

The most useful sentence in the document turns out to be a definition. Zero unexplained breaks lets a break with a written explanation through; it does not let an unresolved break through. In April 2028 two loans sit exactly in that gap, and the plan gives the User Representative something to refuse against.

Not a launch date. A window in which two systems are both live and both have to be right, ending in one weekend in which the old one stops. The dates are chosen against the institution's own calendar, not against the project's convenience.

The plan for changing how people work, as opposed to the plan for changing the software. Training, roles, procedures, communication, and who is angry and why. Most projects that fail after go-live fail here, in a document nobody had four hours to write.

notes: Quality assurance versus quality control

Quality control asks whether the product is right. Quality assurance asks whether the process that produces it is being followed. Deming does the second, reports to the Steering Committee and not to the Project Manager, and sets the standard rather than signing the result — because an independent reviewer who reports to the person he reviews is a decoration.
The one row where the Project Manager is accountable

Whether this project's own controls exist, are used and do anything. The Core Team is responsible for producing the evidence; the Solution Provider, who owns the quality of what gets built, is merely informed. It surprises every Solution Provider it is said to.
Findings are not blame

Cost performance 0.90 — ninety cents of value for every euro out of the door. It is a ratio, so it forecasts: EUR 8.4 m divided by 0.90 is EUR 9.33 m.
The Project Owner writes it in the corner of a page and underlines it once. Nine hundred and thirty-three thousand euro is not a variance; it is a small project.
What it does to the date

Baselined go-live 15 May 2028. Forecast on this trend, 15 June. One month, against a threshold in the Handbook that sends anything over ten working days to the Committee — which is why the recovery plan is on the agenda of the twenty-third whether or not anybody likes its shape by then.

Not a mood. The colour exists to tell the Committee when to spend its attention: does this project need attention before the twenty-third? Yes. Then the colour is decided and the argument was about a word.
notes: What earned value is

Three numbers on the same scale. Planned value is what the plan said would be finished by today, priced. Earned value is what actually is finished, priced the same way. Actual cost is what has been paid. Comparing the first two gives schedule; comparing the last two gives cost.
Why it beats percentage complete
Because it prices progress instead of asking how people feel about it. A task at ninety per cent contributes nothing to earned value until somebody who did not build it says it is finished.
The forecast is the frightening part

A ratio applied to the whole budget turns a bad quarter into a number for 2028. It is not a prediction of doom; it is what happens if nothing changes, which is exactly the question a steering committee exists to answer.

extra: Why the two break

A three billion euro EFSF bond matured on Tuesday 25 April and the refinancing settles today. For loans on the old pooling arrangement the allocation of funding cost reaches them a day late: the treasury feed publishes at close, the platform consumes at six in the morning, and for those two the recomputation lands after close. The platform and the treasury system therefore disagree about the carry, and the report says so in a footnote instead of balancing.
Whose it is

The feed, not the platform — and at ten past seven in the morning nobody cares whose it is. The success criterion says same day. The report says otherwise. Somebody owns that sentence, and on both occasions it is the Business Manager who says so first, which is the only way this ever goes well.
Data or software

In April 2027 the answer is data: the matching key is the old EFSF loan reference, and about three hundred were re-issued in 2014 with a different check digit. That does not make it acceptable. It makes it a question with three possible answers — three hundred rows of data, a matching rule, or both — that has to be answered by Friday, costed, and then decided by somebody.
The fix, in 2028

Force an intraday recomputation for the pooled loans and re-run at eleven. Not this morning: four days of work and a re-test. Four days from 27 April is a clean re-test on 3 May — inside the acceptance window, outside the parallel run.
What the criterion actually says

AC-04: same-day reconciliation, tolerance zero unexplained breaks. These two are explained. They are not resolved. The tolerance only uses one of those words, which is why the User Representative can refuse without inventing a reason.
Nine hundred and ninety-eight is not a thousand
Two years earlier, in a meeting about a plan for 2028, she said that the difference between nearly right and right is the whole of her job. She was two years early and off by nothing at all.
notes: What reconciliation means here

Proving that two independent systems agree about the same money on the same day. If they disagree, one of them is wrong, and until somebody knows which, the institution does not actually know what it paid.
A risk that has already happened
On 11 April 2027 the two-day reconciliation is not a risk any more. R-13 closes and the same fact opens as an issue, because something that has already happened has no likelihood left to score.
Why a footnote is not enough

A break recorded in a footnote exists only in the head of the person who wrote it. Both breaks go into the Issue Log before nine in the morning, one entry each, owner named, target date — whatever the room then decides about acceptance.

Four out of five today, and none of the five signed off, because signing them off takes a year: one working day across fourteen disbursements in a quiet July is not one working day across a quarter-end, an August and the week before Christmas.

Where CR-014 is explained: a telephone call from a cabinet on 13 May 2027, one hundred and forty-five person-days, EUR 392,000 at 2027 prices, six weeks of delay to a release that ran into the parallel run. Postponed by decision D-09. Anybody picking it up in 2029 should re-estimate it against a data model that has changed twice since, not re-open it.

Forty-one entries in the register plus nine new ones from the closing session, grouped under six headings and sent to every project manager in the building rather than filed. Including the one about designing a migration to be run twenty times, written by a man in the week he left.

Benefit measurement across the 2029 reporting year — named owner, named cadence, named date, or it is a wish with a heading on it. Lending Operations, quarterly, out of the division's own operational reporting, from the third quarter of 2028; the full-year statement for 2029 goes to the Corporate Investment Board in the first quarter of 2030. A follow-up project to onboard the backstop within six weeks of ratification. And two product templates deferred out of Release 1, which are maintenance and not a project.

body.h: Performance of the Core Team and the contractor
body.t: Evaluated with the contractor in the room, because otherwise what gets written down is gossip. Both releases on their baselined dates, the second one after both sides lost an architect. The configuration engine is better than the tender described. The migration estimate was optimistic, and both signatures on it are in the room. In the contractor's own words: a good project and a bad estimate, in that order, and nobody should print it the other way round.

body.h: Who this document is actually for
body.t: Not the people who were in the room. In January 2029 a project manager appointed to the backstop onboarding project pulls it out of the archive on her second day and asks what it cost to postpone CR-014. Section 3.3 for why, section 7 for what was learned, the Change Log for the money. That is the only thing it was ever for.

sign: Signed by the Project Manager 28 Jul 2028, countersigned by the Project Owner in September
notes: What a Project-End Report is

The account of what happened, written while the people who know are still there, for people who are not. It is not a celebration and not a defence: conclusions balanced, based on a thorough analysis of the facts.
Why it cannot state the benefits

The platform is the output. Straight-through processing is the outcome. The benefit is a number somebody reads in 2030. Three different things, and only the first was ever the project's to finish. A report claiming what it cannot show is worse than one saying measurement continues, because the first kind is found out by somebody who was not in the room.
There is no gate after this

Three phase gates exist: Ready for Planning, Ready for Executing, Ready for Closing. There is no fourth. The last check on the Closing sheet asks whether the project is ready to be closed, and its answer travels to the Project Owner rather than to a committee. Every approval in twenty-six months opened a door; this one shuts one, and nobody has written a ceremony for that.

t: Six headings on the board
sub: Written up in conference room Schuman at ten past two on a twenty-eight degree afternoon by a man who does not sit down again for two hours — with the forty-one-entry register open beside them, and two pages from somebody else's project that have been in Henry Gantt's drawer since 2023.
head: Lessons Learned · forty-one entries in the register, and nine more from one hot afternoon

cols.t: From the last project — the two pages Gantt keeps

cards.t: Business experts promised part-time delivered part of part-time
cards.d: One of the two pages of lessons learned from the collateral register replacement, three years earlier. It is read out at the very first meeting about CASTOR, before there is a project, and again at the kick-off. It happens to CASTOR anyway — but this time it is critical success factor number one in the Handbook, and it is R-05 in the Risk Log.

cards.t: Page two — everything else
cards.d: A Project-End Report from a project nobody in the room worked on, pulled out of the archive because somebody remembered it existed. This is what a lessons learned register is for, and it is the only proof that it works.

cards.t: Entry 19 · Migration rehearsal effort underestimated
cards.d: Written in the week it happened, which is the discipline. What the register does not say is that the architect said so in November and the analyst assumed he was managing it himself — and he was not managing it, he was rewriting it. That sentence only exists because two people contradicted each other in a hot room in July.

cards.t: Entry 22 · We designed the migration to be run once, correctly. We ran it four times. Design it to be run twenty times.
cards.d: The last entry the lead architect wrote before he left, and the only polite thing he wrote that month. In three years somebody starting a project none of these people has thought of will read it and it will save them a hundred days. That is the part that outlives everybody, and it is a folder path.

cards.t: The cabinets were never on the Stakeholder Matrix
cards.d: Nobody puts them there, because nobody thinks of them as stakeholders until one of them telephones. Recommendation: map the cabinets from Initiating, and give them a route that is not the telephone.

cards.t: CR-014 · A verbal scope request buys no estimating effort until it is on a form
cards.d: A telephone call on 13 May 2027: backstop screens in Release 2, please, and the word small used three times. Two days of everybody's life went into it before one word was written down. Then it became a Change Request Form, a line in the Change Log and a Steering Committee decision on the twenty-sixth: postponed, decision D-09. One sentence for a stranger, and it cost two days that somebody else can now have free.

cards.t: Half our response to key-person risk was a person
cards.d: R-07 was in the Risk Log from June 2026 with strategy Reduce and two actions: a key-person clause in the contract, and the seconded architect shadowing the design authority. The clause worked — the contractor's own platform architect resigned in April 2027 and there was a named replacement and three weeks of handover at their cost, because somebody paid for that sentence in 2026. Then the seconded architect resigned, and there was no clause, because he was the clause. One half was written into a contract; the other half was never written down anywhere.

cards.t: A response that is never exercised is not a response
cards.d: Fifteen person-days of knowledge transfer, task 4.7, target 18 December 2026. Two of the three modules were transferred. The third was the product configuration engine, and it was still scheduled nine months after its target date, on the risk at the top of the log.

cards.t: Acceptance criteria have to be written by somebody who does the job
cards.d: The User Representative's own lesson, and she calls it small: on 27 April 2028, nine hundred and ninety-eight loans reconciled and two did not, in the week of a three billion euro rollover, and she refused. Somebody told her there was a process for refusing and, to her surprise, there was. If she had not made a nuisance of herself in 2026 she would have had nothing to refuse against, and she would have signed.

cards.t: The argument about which plan owns retraining was worth having in Planning
cards.d: Three weeks of 2026, and not politely: Transition Plan or Business Implementation Plan. It went into the Business Implementation Plan, under the Business Manager, with the Project Owner accountable — and afterwards it never once needed change control.

cards.t: The person running the session should not be the person the session is about
cards.d: Twenty-six months of this belong to the Project Manager. If he holds the pen, half the room is kind to him and the other half aims. Somebody else takes the pen and he answers when he is asked.

cards.t: What happens after us
cards.d: Three things, grouped in that order and sent to every project manager in the building rather than filed: benefit measurement across the 2029 reporting year; a follow-up project to onboard the backstop within six weeks of ratification, reusing the configuration engine and re-estimating CR-014 rather than re-opening it; and two deferred product templates, which are maintenance and not a project.

notes: What a lessons learned register is

A running list, written the week the thing happens rather than reconstructed at the end. Forty-one entries by July 2028. The closing session adds nine new ones — and eight of those nine exist only because two people contradicted each other out loud.
Why it is done eight weeks after go-live and not in September

September gives better answers and gives them to nobody: the analyst goes back to her division on Monday, the contractor's project manager is on a plane at seven tonight, and two testers leave the same day. A worse answer from the people who were there beats a better one from an empty room.
Why a steering committee sits in a room about what went wrong

Because a lesson that stays inside the project it came from is a memory. The four people on that committee sit on six other projects between them, and the Architecture Office takes two of these into a target architecture review in October. That is not manners; it is the only road they travel on.
